content: Cardiopulmonary arrest in pediatric patients frequently leads to either death or survival accompanied by significant brain injury. Therapeutic hypothermia, which involves reducing the core body temperature to a range of 32°C to 34°C, has been shown to mitigate brain injury during the post-resuscitation period. This approach has demonstrated efficacy in neonates with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy and in adults who have experienced cardiopulmonary arrest due to witnessed ventricular fibrillation. However, the impact of therapeutic hypothermia on pediatric patients following cardiopulmonary arrest remains uncertain. The objective of this study was to evaluate the clinical effectiveness of therapeutic hypothermia in children who have experienced cardiopulmonary arrest. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Anaesthesia Review Group Specialized Register, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, Ovid CINAHL, Ovid BIOSIS, and Web of Science, covering literature up to December 2011. Additionally, trial registry databases were reviewed for ongoing studies, and international experts in therapeutic hypothermia and pediatric critical care were consulted to identify further published and unpublished research. The inclusion criteria for this review specified randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared therapeutic hypothermia with normothermia or standard care in children aged 24 hours to 18 years who had experienced cardiopulmonary arrest. Two independent authors assessed the eligibility of articles for inclusion in the review. No studies meeting the inclusion criteria were identified. However, four ongoing randomized controlled trials were noted, which may provide data for future analysis. Eighteen non-randomized studies were excluded from the review. Among these, three studies compared therapeutic hypothermia with standard therapy but found no significant differences in mortality rates or the proportion of children achieving favorable neurological outcomes. These findings were presented narratively. In conclusion, this review does not provide sufficient evidence to support or refute the use of therapeutic hypothermia in pediatric patients following cardiopulmonary arrest. Further randomized controlled trials are necessary to establish the clinical efficacy of this intervention, and the results of ongoing trials will be evaluated when they become available.
